questions.question_text: The apostrophe rule: when a syllable beginning with a, o or e follows another syllable, it is separated by an apostrophe, $\text{dì} + \text{èr} \rightarrow ?$. How is 第二 ("second") spelled in pinyin?

options.A: dìèr
options.B: dìer
options.C: dièr

questions.explanation: Without the apostrophe, readers could be unsure where the syllable boundary falls; in dì'èr the mark makes clear that the syllables are dì and èr, not di + er or die + r. Compare 第一 (dìyī), which needs no apostrophe, and 女儿 (nǚ'ér), "daughter", which does.

questions.question_text: Use $\text{number} + \text{measure word} + \text{noun}$ twice to say "I want to buy two tickets and one map" (地图 dìtú).

options.A: 我要买两张车票和一张地图。(wǒ yào mǎi liǎng zhāng chēpiào hé yì zhāng dìtú.)
options.B: 我要买二张车票和一张地图。(wǒ yào mǎi èr zhāng chēpiào hé yì zhāng dìtú.)
options.C: 我要买两张车票和一杯地图。(wǒ yào mǎi liǎng zhāng chēpiào hé yì bēi dìtú.)
options.D: 我要买两车票张和一地图张。(wǒ yào mǎi liǎng chēpiào zhāng hé yì dìtú zhāng.)

questions.explanation: Each noun gets its own number + measure word block, both with 张 (zhāng) for flat things; "two" is 两 (liǎng) before a measure word, and 和 (hé) links the two noun phrases. 杯 (bēi) counts cups, not maps.

questions.question_text: Which formula fits "She does not like history very much": $S + \text{bú tài} + V + O$?

options.A: 她不喜欢太历史。(tā bù xǐhuan tài lìshǐ.)
options.B: 她喜欢不太历史。(tā xǐhuan bú tài lìshǐ.)
options.C: 不太她喜欢历史。(bú tài tā xǐhuan lìshǐ.)
options.D: 她不太喜欢历史。(tā bú tài xǐhuan lìshǐ.)

questions.explanation: 不太 (bú tài, "not very") modifies the verb and goes directly in front of 喜欢 (xǐhuan), after the subject. 不 becomes bú because 太 (tài) has the fourth tone. Another example: 我不太想去 (wǒ bú tài xiǎng qù), "I do not much want to go."

questions.question_text: Compounds are built from meaningful parts: 飞机 (fēijī) = 飞 (fēi, "fly") + 机 (jī, "machine"), "airplane". Using $\text{jī (machine)} + \text{chǎng (field)}$, what does 机场 (jīchǎng) mean?

options.A: Train station
options.B: Airport
options.C: Mobile phone

questions.explanation: A "field for flying machines" is an airport: 机场 (jīchǎng). The same morpheme 机 (jī) appears in 手机 (shǒujī, "hand machine" = mobile phone), which shows how a few building-block characters multiply vocabulary. Example: 机场在哪里？(jīchǎng zài nǎlǐ?), "Where is the airport?"

questions.question_text: In the reply "好吧，我帮你找。" (hǎo ba, wǒ bāng nǐ zhǎo.), what does the particle 吧 (ba) do in 好吧 (hǎo ba)?

options.A: It turns the sentence into a yes/no question
options.B: It softens the statement and signals a concession, roughly "OK, then"
options.C: It marks the action as finished

questions.explanation: Grammar point: the sentence-final particle 吧 (ba). It softens a statement, suggestion or agreement (好吧 (hǎo ba) "all right, then"; 我们走吧 wǒmen zǒu ba, "let's go"). A yes/no question is built with 吗 (ma), completed actions are marked differently, and plurals use 们 (men).

questions.question_text: In "我的手机不见了。" (wǒ de shǒujī bú jiàn le.), what does the final 了 (le) signal?

options.A: A new situation or change of state: the phone has now disappeared
options.B: That the sentence is a question
options.C: That the phone belongs to someone else
options.D: That the speaker wants to find the phone

questions.explanation: Grammar point: sentence-final 了 (le) for a change of state. It reports that something has become the case, so 手机不见了 (shǒujī bú jiàn le) means "the phone is (now) missing". Another example: 我不想去了 (wǒ bù xiǎng qù le), "I do not want to go any more."

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "He likes music, and he also likes history"?

options.A: 他喜欢音乐，也喜欢历史。(tā xǐhuan yīnyuè, yě xǐhuan lìshǐ.)
options.B: 他喜欢音乐，喜欢也历史。(tā xǐhuan yīnyuè, xǐhuan yě lìshǐ.)
options.C: 他喜欢音乐，喜欢历史也。(tā xǐhuan yīnyuè, xǐhuan lìshǐ yě.)
options.D: 他喜欢也音乐，喜欢历史。(tā xǐhuan yě yīnyuè, xǐhuan lìshǐ.)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: the adverb 也 (yě) in a second clause. When the subject is dropped in the second clause, 也 (yě) still goes directly before the verb it modifies: ...，也喜欢历史 (yě xǐhuan lìshǐ). It can never follow the verb or sit between the verb and its object. Another example: 我喝茶，也喝咖啡 (wǒ hē chá, yě hē kāfēi).

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "I am a student and he is a teacher"?

options.A: 我是学生和他是老师。(wǒ shì xuésheng hé tā shì lǎoshī.)
options.B: 我和是学生他是老师。(wǒ hé shì xuésheng tā shì lǎoshī.)
options.C: 我是学生，他是老师。(wǒ shì xuésheng, tā shì lǎoshī.)
options.D: 我是学生和他是老师吗。(wǒ shì xuésheng hé tā shì lǎoshī ma.)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: 和 (hé) joins nouns or pronouns, not whole clauses. Two clauses are simply placed side by side, separated by a comma. 和 (hé) works in 我喜欢数学和音乐 (wǒ xǐhuan shùxué hé yīnyuè), "I like mathematics and music", where it links two nouns.

questions.question_text: Choose the best translation of "我在找我的手机。" (wǒ zài zhǎo wǒ de shǒujī.)

options.A: I am at my phone and I search.
options.B: I am looking for my phone.
options.C: My phone is at the place where I search.
options.D: I will look for my phone tomorrow.

questions.explanation: Grammar point: 在 (zài) before a verb as a progressive marker. When no place follows, 在 (zài) + verb means the action is in progress: 在找 (zài zhǎo), "is looking for". Only when a place follows (在书店看书 (zài shūdiàn kàn shū)) does 在 (zài) mean "at". Another example: 她在吃饭 (tā zài chī fàn), "She is eating."

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "The key is on the table, and the ticket is in the wallet"?

options.A: 钥匙在桌子上，车票在钱包里。(yàoshi zài zhuōzi shàng, chēpiào zài qiánbāo lǐ.)
options.B: 钥匙在桌子里，车票在钱包上。(yàoshi zài zhuōzi lǐ, chēpiào zài qiánbāo shàng.)
options.C: 钥匙在上桌子，车票在里钱包。(yàoshi zài shàng zhuōzi, chēpiào zài lǐ qiánbāo.)
options.D: 钥匙桌子上在，车票钱包里在。(yàoshi zhuōzi shàng zài, chēpiào qiánbāo lǐ zài.)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: localizers (position words) 上 (shàng) and 里 (lǐ). They follow the noun: 在 (zài) + place + 上 (shàng)/里 (lǐ), and the choice depends on the physical relation (surface versus container). Swapping them changes the meaning to "inside the table" and "on the wallet"; putting them first is ungrammatical.

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "I want to drink three cups of water"?

options.A: 我想喝三杯水。(wǒ xiǎng hē sān bēi shuǐ.)
options.B: 我想喝三水杯。(wǒ xiǎng hē sān shuǐ bēi.)
options.C: 我想喝杯三水。(wǒ xiǎng hē bēi sān shuǐ.)
options.D: 我想三喝杯水。(wǒ xiǎng sān hē bēi shuǐ.)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: measure words. A number cannot sit directly before a noun; the pattern is number + measure word + noun, with 杯 (bēi) for cups of liquid. Here 想 (xiǎng) also precedes the verb 喝 (hē). Another example: 一张地图 (yì zhāng dìtú), "a map".

questions.question_text: A group contains two men and three women. Which pronoun is normally used for "they" when saying "They are all students"?

options.A: 她们 (tāmen, women only)
options.B: 它们 (tāmen, things only)
options.C: 他 (tā, singular)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: the plural pronoun 他们 (tāmen) is the default for a mixed or unspecified group; 她们 (tāmen) is used only for groups made up entirely of women, and 它们 (tāmen) for things or animals. All three are pronounced tāmen, and only the written character differs.

questions.question_text: Which sentence is the polite way to ask a stranger "Excuse me, where is the airport?"

options.A: 请问，机场在哪里？(qǐngwèn, jīchǎng zài nǎlǐ?)
options.B: 机场请问在哪里？(jīchǎng qǐngwèn zài nǎlǐ?)
options.C: 请问，机场在哪里吗？(qǐngwèn, jīchǎng zài nǎlǐ ma?)
options.D: 请问，在哪里机场？(qǐngwèn, zài nǎlǐ jīchǎng?)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: the polite opener 请问 (qǐngwèn, "may I ask") placed at the very start, followed by a normal question 机场在哪里 (jīchǎng zài nǎlǐ). Because 哪里 (nǎlǐ) is a question word, no 吗 (ma) is added. Another example: 请问，洗手间在哪里？(qǐngwèn, xǐshǒujiān zài nǎlǐ?)

questions.question_text: Someone asks "你的车票在哪里？" (nǐ de chēpiào zài nǎlǐ?). Which is the correct short answer for "It is in my phone"?

options.A: 是手机里。(shì shǒujī lǐ.)
options.B: 手机里在。(shǒujī lǐ zài.)
options.C: 在手机里。(zài shǒujī lǐ.)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: answering a location question with 在 (zài) + place + position word. The subject is dropped because it is already known, and the verb 在 (zài) is kept. 是 (shì) would identify instead of locating. Another example: 在桌子上 (zài zhuōzi shàng), "On the table."

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "She wants to eat snacks at the supermarket"?

options.A: 她想在超市吃零食。(tā xiǎng zài chāoshì chī língshí.)
options.B: 她在想超市吃零食。(tā zài xiǎng chāoshì chī língshí.)
options.C: 她吃想在超市零食。(tā chī xiǎng zài chāoshì língshí.)
options.D: 她想吃在超市零食。(tā xiǎng chī zài chāoshì língshí.)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: the modal verb 想 (xiǎng, "want to") comes before the whole verb phrase, and the phrase itself keeps its order 在 (zài) + place + verb + object. Putting 在 (zài) directly after the subject (她在想 (tā zài xiǎng)...) would turn 想 (xiǎng) into "is thinking". Another example: 我想在家看书 (wǒ xiǎng zài jiā kàn shū).

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "I did not go to the supermarket yesterday" (a single completed event)?

options.A: 我昨天不去超市。(wǒ zuótiān bú qù chāoshì.)
options.B: 我昨天没去超市。(wǒ zuótiān méi qù chāoshì.)
options.C: 我没昨天去超市。(wǒ méi zuótiān qù chāoshì.)
options.D: 我昨天去没超市。(wǒ zuótiān qù méi chāoshì.)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: negation with 没 (méi) versus 不 (bù). 没 (méi) negates events that did not happen (completed or past), while 不 (bù) negates habits, intentions and the future: 我明天不去超市 (wǒ míngtiān bú qù chāoshì), "I will not go tomorrow." Both stand directly in front of the verb.

questions.question_text: Which phrase correctly says "the second platform"?

options.A: 第两站台 (dì liǎng zhàntái)
options.B: 二第站台 (èr dì zhàntái)
options.C: 第二站台 (dì'èr zhàntái)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: ordinal numbers. 第 (dì) goes before the number to form an ordinal, and the number "two" is 二 (èr) in ordinals; 两 (liǎng) is reserved for counting before measure words (两张车票 (liǎng zhāng chēpiào)). Another example: 第一站台 (dìyī zhàntái), "the first platform".

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "My country is Brazil" (it identifies the country)?

options.A: 我的国家在巴西。(wǒ de guójiā zài Bāxī.)
options.B: 我的国家是巴西。(wǒ de guójiā shì Bāxī.)
options.C: 我的国家是巴西人。(wǒ de guójiā shì Bāxī rén.)
options.D: 我国家的是巴西。(wǒ guójiā de shì Bāxī.)

questions.explanation: Grammar point: 是 (shì) for identity with a country noun. 是 (shì) equates two nouns, 巴西 (Bāxī) names the country, while 巴西人 (Bāxī rén) means a Brazilian person; 在 (zài) would say that the country is located in Brazil. Another example: 美国是我的国家 (Měiguó shì wǒ de guójiā).

questions.question_text: Which reading strategy best helps you distinguish 哪 (nǎ, "which / where") from 那 (nà, "that")?

options.A: Count the strokes, because 哪 (nǎ) always has more strokes than the sentence needs
options.B: Notice the mouth radical 口 (kǒu) in 哪 (nǎ), typical of question words, and check whether the slot calls for a question
options.C: Treat them as interchangeable since both are pronounced the same
options.D: Look at whether the sentence contains 们 (men)

questions.explanation: 哪 (nǎ, third tone) belongs to the question-word family (哪里 nǎlǐ, 哪儿 nǎr, 哪国 nǎ guó) and has the mouth radical 口 (kǒu), while 那 (nà, fourth tone) is the demonstrative "that" (那里 nàlǐ, "there"). Tone and radical together prevent the mix-up.

questions.question_text: A Portuguese speaker worries about conjugating 去 (qù, "to go") for each person and tense. Which statement is correct?

options.A: 去 (qù) adds a suffix for the third person, as in English "goes"
options.B: 去 (qù) takes 们 (men) when the subject is plural, giving 去们 (qù men)
options.C: 去 (qù) changes its tone by the gender of the subject
options.D: 去 (qù) stays the same for every person (我去 (wǒ qù), 她去 (tā qù), 他们去 (tāmen qù)); time is shown by words such as 今天 (jīntiān) or 明天 (míngtiān)

questions.explanation: Chinese verbs are not conjugated for person, number or gender. Meaning of time comes from time words (今天 jīntiān, "today"; 明天 míngtiān, "tomorrow") and particles such as 了 (le). Example: 我去超市 (wǒ qù chāoshì), 她去超市 (tā qù chāoshì), 他们去超市 (tāmen qù chāoshì) use identical verbs.

questions.question_text: Which practice routine best fixes the choice between bù and bú?

options.A: Always write bú, since it is the more common spelling
options.B: Memorize bú only for the word 是 (shì) and use bù everywhere else
options.C: Memorize the rule by the tone of the next syllable and drill contrasting pairs such as 不是 (bú shì) / 不去 (bú qù) against 不吃 (bù chī) / 不想 (bù xiǎng)
options.D: Ignore the change, because native speakers do not use it

questions.explanation: 不 is bù by default and becomes bú before a fourth-tone syllable (不是 bú shì, 不去 bú qù, 不太 bú tài), but stays bù before tones 1, 2 and 3 (不吃 bù chī, 不想 bù xiǎng). Drilling minimal pairs trains the ear and the rule together.

questions.question_text: A learner pronounces 你好 (nǐ hǎo) with two full dipping tones and sounds stilted. What is the best correction?

options.A: Drop the tone of the second syllable completely (nǐ hao)
options.B: Change the written pinyin to ní hǎo
options.C: Raise the first syllable like a second tone (ní hǎo) while still writing nǐ hǎo
options.D: Say both syllables with the first tone

questions.explanation: Third-tone sandhi: when two third tones meet, the first one is spoken as a rising second tone, but the standard spelling keeps the original tone marks. This is why a native speaker says ní hǎo even though dictionaries print nǐ hǎo. Another example: 很好 (hěn hǎo) is spoken hén hǎo.

questions.question_text: In which situation is saying 我也是中国人 (wǒ yě shì Zhōngguó rén) natural?

options.A: As the very first sentence when introducing yourself to a group
options.B: When you want to say you are not Chinese
options.C: Right after someone else has said they are Chinese, and you are Chinese too
options.D: When asking someone else if they are Chinese

questions.explanation: 也 (yě, "also") only makes sense in relation to a previous statement: someone is already known to share the property. In a first introduction you say 我是中国人 (wǒ shì Zhōngguó rén). Another example: A: 我是韩国人 (wǒ shì Hánguó rén)。 B: 我也是韩国人 (wǒ yě shì Hánguó rén).

questions.question_text: Which question would be naturally answered with 我在书店。(wǒ zài shūdiàn.)?

options.A: 你去哪儿？(nǐ qù nǎr?)
options.B: 你是哪国人？(nǐ shì nǎ guó rén?)
options.C: 你喜欢什么课？(nǐ xǐhuan shénme kè?)

questions.explanation: 我在书店 (wǒ zài shūdiàn) states a location, so the matching question asks where you are: 你在哪儿 (nǐ zài nǎr)？ 你去哪儿 (nǐ qù nǎr)？ asks about a destination (answer: 我去书店 (wǒ qù shūdiàn)), 哪国人 (nǎ guó rén) asks about nationality and 什么课 (shénme kè) about a class. Tracking 在 (zài) versus 去 (qù) avoids the most common mix-up with places.

questions.question_text: Why does a Chinese question that contains a question word, such as 你想吃什么？(nǐ xiǎng chī shénme?), not end with 吗 (ma)?

options.A: 吗 (ma) may only follow verbs of motion
options.B: 吗 (ma) is reserved for very formal speech
options.C: The question word already marks the sentence as a question and stands for the missing information, while 吗 (ma) turns a complete statement into a yes/no question
options.D: A question word must always be last, so there is no room for 吗 (ma)

questions.explanation: Two different question strategies: (a) statement + 吗 (ma), e.g. 你想吃零食吗？ (nǐ xiǎng chī língshí ma?), a yes/no question, and (b) a question word in the slot of the unknown information. Combining them is redundant and wrong, as in the errors 你去哪儿吗 (nǐ qù nǎr ma) or 你喜欢什么课吗 (nǐ xǐhuan shénme kè ma).

questions.question_text: You know that 巴西人 (Bāxī rén) means "a Brazilian". Extending the same pattern to a city, how do you say "a person from Beijing" (北京 Běijīng)?

options.A: 北京国人 (Běijīng guó rén)
options.B: 北京人 (Běijīng rén)
options.C: 人北京 (rén Běijīng)

questions.explanation: The pattern place + 人 (rén, "person") generalizes beyond countries: 北京人 (Běijīng rén), 上海人 (Shànghǎi rén). 国 (guó) is part of some country names only, 们 (men) pluralizes people pronouns, and the head noun 人 (rén) always comes last.

questions.question_text: Which slot order is the safest when building a long sentence such as "Tomorrow I go to the cinema with a friend to see a movie"?

options.A: Subject, action and object, place, time, companion
options.B: Place, time, subject, companion, action
options.C: Companion, action, subject, time, place
options.D: Time, subject, companion with 一起 (yìqǐ), 去 (qù) + place, then the action and object

questions.explanation: Chinese tends to put context before the main verb: time and subject first, then manner and companion phrases, then 去 (qù) + place, and finally the action and object. Result: 明天我和朋友一起去电影院看电影 (míngtiān wǒ hé péngyou yìqǐ qù diànyǐngyuàn kàn diànyǐng). Trailing time or place phrases are usually wrong.

questions.question_text: Which is the best strategy for learning measure words such as 张 (zhāng) and 杯 (bēi)?

options.A: Learn each noun together with its measure word as a chunk, for example 一张车票 (yì zhāng chēpiào) and 一杯茶 (yì bēi chá)
options.B: Use 张 (zhāng) for every noun, since it is the universal measure word
options.C: Skip measure words, because a number can go directly before any noun
options.D: Memorize a list of measure words without any nouns

questions.explanation: Measure words depend on the noun (张 (zhāng) for flat objects such as tickets and maps, 杯 (bēi) for cups of drinks, 本 (běn) for books), so they are best stored in chunks: 一张车票 (yì zhāng chēpiào), 一杯茶 (yì bēi chá). A number cannot normally go directly in front of a noun.

questions.question_text: In which situation is the opener 请问 (qǐngwèn, "may I ask") appropriate?

options.A: To thank someone after receiving help
options.B: Before asking a stranger for information, for example where the station is
options.C: To say goodbye politely

questions.explanation: 请问 (qǐngwèn) literally means "please ask / may I ask" and introduces a polite question to someone you do not know. Thanks is 谢谢 (xièxie), goodbye is 再见 (zàijiàn), and "yes" repeats the verb or uses 是 (shì). Example: 请问，火车站在哪里？(qǐngwèn, huǒchēzhàn zài nǎlǐ?)

questions.question_text: 火车站 (huǒchēzhàn), 地铁站 (dìtiězhàn) and 站台 (zhàntái) all contain 站 (zhàn). What is the best inference about 站 (zhàn)?

options.A: It relates to a stop or station, a place where vehicles halt
options.B: It means ticket
options.C: It means vehicle

questions.explanation: Recognizing recurring components speeds up vocabulary: 站 (zhàn) carries the idea of a station or a standing place, so 火车站 (huǒchēzhàn) is the train station, 地铁站 (dìtiězhàn) is the subway station and 站台 (zhàntái) is the platform. The vehicle parts here are 火车 (huǒchē, "train") and 地铁 (dìtiě, "subway").

questions.question_text: What does 他不常去书店 (tā bù cháng qù shūdiàn) imply?

options.A: He never goes to the bookstore
options.B: He goes to the bookstore sometimes, but not often
options.C: He goes to the bookstore every day
options.D: He went to the bookstore only yesterday

questions.explanation: 不常 (bù cháng, "not often") lowers the frequency without ruling the action out; "never" would need a different word. It sits between the subject and verb like all frequency expressions. Compare 他很少去书店 (tā hěn shǎo qù shūdiàn), "He rarely goes to the bookstore."

questions.question_text: The tone mark in the third-tone syllable 酒 (jiǔ) as in 酒店 (jiǔdiàn, "hotel") goes on the u. Which spelling places it correctly?

options.A: jǐu
options.B: jiǔ
options.C: jiù

questions.explanation: Pinyin rule: a tone mark goes on the vowel a, e or o if present; in the combinations iu and ui it goes on the second (last) vowel. So the third tone appears as jiǔ, not jǐu, and 对 (duì) is written with the mark on i. The option jiù carries the fourth tone instead.

questions.question_text: If you send a message in pinyin only, "Tā shì dàxuésheng", what information from the characters is lost?

options.A: The tone of the verb 是 (shì)
options.B: The fact that the sentence is a statement
options.C: The order of the words
options.D: Whether the subject is "he" or "she" (他 (tā) or 她 (tā))

questions.explanation: 他 (tā) and 她 (tā) are both pronounced tā, so only the written characters (人 (rén) versus 女 (nǚ) radical) distinguish them. Tones, word order and sentence type remain visible in pinyin. This is why context or a name is needed when you only type pinyin.

questions.question_text: After saying 我不太喜欢体育 (wǒ bú tài xǐhuan tǐyù), a speaker adds 你呢？(nǐ ne?). What exactly is the question?

options.A: Do you like physical education, or what do you think of it?
options.B: Where is the physical education class?
options.C: Are you a student?

questions.explanation: 呢 (ne) after a pronoun hands the previous topic back: "and you, how about you?" Here the topic is liking physical education. It differs from 吗 (ma), which creates a new yes/no question. Another example: 我喜欢音乐，她呢？(wǒ xǐhuan yīnyuè, tā ne?), "I like music; and she?"
